packet.headline_seed: Why are devastating mice plagues happening in Australia?
packet.description_seed: Crops are being ravaged and homes are being invaded by the rodents - and it’s costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars.

what: Why are devastating mice plagues happening in Australia?

clean_source_blocks.text: Crops are being ravaged and homes are being invaded by the rodents - and it’s costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars.

A mouse plague has taken hold over large swathes of Australian farmland, and it is costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars. BBC Australia Journalist Lana Lam investigates why the nation is being terrorised by rodents - and whether there is an end in sight. Hundreds paddle out at Bondi beach to commemorate the shooting victims from Sunday's attack. Matilda, 10, was mourned by family, friends, and the community in Sydney after she was killed in the Bondi shooting on Sunday. Rabbi Ulman, the father-in-law of British-born Rabbi Eli Schlanger, said he hoped his son-in-law knew how loved he was. The mother of 10-year-old Matilda, the youngest victim of the Bondi Beach attack, paid tribute to her daughter at a flower memorial on Tuesday evening.

Got a mouse in your house? That thought alone may terrify you. Now imagine if mice were scampering through your house, rummaging in your pantry or even running across your face at night. That sounds like the stuff of nightmares, but it’s what many Australians have experienced when living through a mouse plague. Mouse plagues can be economically and psychologically devastating, particularly for rural communities. This is because mice destroy crops, spread disease and damage the natural environment. Currently, farmers across two Australian states are battling a potential mouse plague. And it’s an unsettling reminder of the mouse plagues of 2020 and 2021 that ravaged farms and rural communities across Australia’s east coast. So what’s causing this latest plague? And how are farmers coping?

Farmers in Australia are battling a mouse plague with large numbers swarming farms and damaging crops Experts warn the infestation could severely impact Australia's $3 billion grain export industry and local communities Previous plagues in 2020 and 2021 caused $1 billion in damages Multiple parts of Australia have been hit with large numbers of mice, with farmers being forced to either shoot the animals or burn damaged crops, according to multiple reports. According to 9 News, a number of videos posted to social media show massive swarms of mice along farmlands in Western and Southern Australia, while news.com.au reported on Wednesday, April 28 that some clips captured hordes covering an entire road and more rodents surrounding a grain silo.

[Lähde: The Conversation]
Got a mouse in your house? That thought alone may terrify you.

Now imagine if mice were scampering through your house, rummaging in your pantry or even running across your face at night.

That sounds like the stuff of nightmares, but it’s what many Australians have experienced when living through a mouse plague.

Mouse plagues can be economically and psychologically devastating, particularly for rural communities. This is because mice destroy crops, spread disease and damage the natural environment.

Currently, farmers across two Australian states are battling a potential mouse plague. And it’s an unsettling reminder of the mouse plagues of 2020 and 2021 that ravaged farms and rural communities across Australia’s east coast.

So what’s causing this latest plague? And how are farmers coping?

Mice have been a part of the Australian environment ever since they arrived with the First Fleet in 1788. Since then, they’ve rapidly bred and spread all around the country.

In some areas, mice populations can reach plague proportions. This means there are at least 800 mice per hectare of land. The first documented mouse plague happened in 1872 in the South Australian town of Saddleworth.

Mouse plagues often occur as a result of cyclones, floods or other weather events that increase rainfall and soil moisture. Good rains help native plants grow, but they also fuel bumper harvests in key grain-growing regions. These are perfect places for mice to breed because they have warmer climates and plentiful food sources, such as grain. In such conditions, mice can prolong their breeding season by several months and even produce several litters each season.

Just this week, farmers in Western Australia and South Australia have been inundated with mice. In parts of WA, some farmers have found 3,000-4,000 burrows in just one hectare of land. And SA mouse numbers are at their highest levels in at least four years.

Unfortunately, the timing could not be worse. That’s because many farmers are about to start seeding – the process of putting seeds into the soil to grow crops – after recent rains. These farmers are now at risk of losing their crops before they even have the chance to germinate.

This all suggests this latest mouse plague could be as bad as the plagues of 2020 and 2021 that affected communities across SA, western Victoria, New South Wales and southern Queensland. Over an 11-month period, millions of mice devoured spring crops and destroyed farm machinery.

payload.title: Hiirivitsaus kurittaa Australian maatiloja ja koteja
payload.summary: Australian maatiloilla laajat hiiriesiintymät ovat tuhonneet satoa, tunkeutuneet koteihin ja aiheuttaneet viljelijöille suuria taloudellisia menetyksiä. Ilmiö koettelee erityisesti maaseutuyhteisöjä ja herättää huolta myös viljantuotannosta.
payload.content:
Australian viljelijät kamppailevat laajoilla maatalousalueilla hiirivitsauksen kanssa, joka tuhoaa satoja, valtaa koteja ja aiheuttaa tiloille jopa satojentuhansien dollarien kustannuksia. Ongelma koskee useita osia maasta, ja lähdeaineiston mukaan seuraukset voivat tuntua sekä paikallisyhteisöissä että Australian merkittävässä viljaviennissä.

## Satoja tuhoutuu ja koteihin tunkeudutaan

Hiirien suuret määrät ovat aiheuttaneet vahinkoja Australian maatiloilla, joilla jyrsijät parveilevat pelloilla ja viljavarastojen ympärillä. Lähdetietojen mukaan viljelijöitä on pakotettu hävittämään eläimiä ja polttamaan vahingoittuneita satoja tilanteen hallitsemiseksi.

Ongelma ei rajoitu peltoihin. Hiiret ovat tunkeutuneet myös koteihin, joissa ne voivat etsiä ruokaa ruokakomeroista ja liikkua sisätiloissa öisin. Tällaiset tilanteet tekevät vitsauksesta paitsi taloudellisen myös henkisesti kuormittavan kokemuksen erityisesti maaseudulla asuville.

Hiirivitsaukset voivat tuhota viljelyksiä, levittää tauteja ja vahingoittaa luonnonympäristöä. Nykyinen tilanne on herättänyt huolta kahdessa Australian osavaltiossa, joissa viljelijät varautuvat mahdollisesti pahenevaan esiintymään.

## Muistot aiemmista tuhoista lisäävät huolta

Tilanne palauttaa mieleen vuosien 2020 ja 2021 hiirivitsaukset, jotka kurittivat maatiloja ja maaseutuyhteisöjä Australian itärannikolla. Tuolloin vahinkojen kerrottiin nousseen jopa miljardiin dollariin.

Nyt esiin noussut uhka kohdistuu myös laajempaan elintarvike- ja vientiketjuun. Arvioiden mukaan voimakas hiiriesiintymä voisi vahingoittaa Australian noin kolmen miljardin dollarin viljavientialaa sekä paikallisia yhteisöjä, joiden toimeentulo riippuu onnistuneesta sadosta.

Sosiaaliseen mediaan julkaistuilla videoilla on kerrottu näkyvän suuria hiirijoukkoja Länsi- ja Etelä-Australian viljelyalueilla. Osa havainnoista on kuvattu teillä ja viljasiilojen läheisyydessä, mikä kertoo ongelman näkyvyydestä arjessa ja tuotantoketjun kriittisissä pisteissä.

Viranomaisten tai tutkijoiden yksiselitteistä arviota vitsauksen kestosta ei lähdeaineistossa esitetä. Selvää kuitenkin on, että viljelijät joutuvat jo nyt tekemään nopeita ja kalliita ratkaisuja sadon, varastojen ja kotien suojelemiseksi.

payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli perustuu valittuihin lähdekatkelmiin. BBC:n aineistossa oli asiaan kuulumatonta Bondi-iskuun liittyvää tekstiä, joka jätettiin pois. Kategoriaksi valittiin Ulkomaat, koska aihe koskee Australiaa eikä Suomea.
